easy.prompt: In attention, what job does the query vector do?

choices.label: A
choices.body: It states what the current position is looking for.

choices.label: B
choices.body: It stores the final output of the whole layer.

choices.label: C
choices.body: It sums all value vectors into one scalar.

choices.label: D
choices.body: It computes the training loss directly.

easy.hint: Next step: match the query against each key, then blend values.
easy.explanation: The query encodes the current position's request; keys advertise each position's content.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: compare the query to every key to get scores. Step 2: softmax turns scores into weights. Step 3: weights blend the value vectors into the output. So the query asks, keys index, values deliver.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The output is built later as a weighted sum; the query is an input to scoring.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Values are blended by weights; the query never sums them itself.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Loss is computed from predictions, not inside the query vector.

easy.prompt: Scaled dot-product attention divides scores by sqrt(d_k) mainly to…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Force all attention weights to be exactly uniform.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Turn dot products into probabilities with no softmax.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Give the model a sense of token order.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Keep softmax inputs moderate so gradients keep flowing.

easy.hint: Next step: recall what huge logits do to softmax gradients.
easy.explanation: Large d_k inflates dot-product magnitudes, which would peak softmax and shrink gradients; scaling stabilizes them.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: q·k variance grows with dimension d_k. Step 2: huge logits make softmax nearly one-hot and saturated. Step 3: saturated softmax has tiny gradients. Dividing by sqrt(d_k) keeps scores in a trainable range.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Scaling stabilizes variance; it never forces uniform weights.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Only softmax creates probabilities; scaling just resizes logits.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Order comes from positional encodings, not from scaling.

easy.prompt: A softmax over key positions always produces…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Raw dot products with no normalization.

choices.label: B
choices.body: A single one-hot vector in every case.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Nonnegative weights that sum to 1 across positions.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Independent scores that can each be 1 at once.

easy.hint: Next step: add up the outputs — what must the total be?
easy.explanation: Softmax normalizes logits into a probability distribution, so weights compete and sum to 1.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: exponentiate each score so all outputs are positive. Step 2: divide by the total so they sum to 1. Step 3: raising one score therefore lowers the others. Outputs are coupled, never independent.

wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Softmax couples outputs through the shared denominator; they cannot all be 1.
wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Dot products are the inputs; softmax normalizes them.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: One-hot only happens when one logit dwarfs the rest, not always.

easy.prompt: The output of one attention head is best described as…

choices.label: A
choices.body: An unweighted average of the key vectors.

choices.label: B
choices.body: A weighted sum of value vectors using attention weights.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The element-wise product of the query and key only.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The single maximum value vector, discarding the rest.

easy.hint: Next step: ask which vectors get summed and which set the weights.
easy.explanation: Output = sum of value vectors weighted by query-key compatibility; keys set weights, values supply content.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: score the query against each key. Step 2: softmax the scores into weights. Step 3: blend the value vectors with those weights. Keys address, values deliver.

wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Query-key products are just scores; values must still be aggregated.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Attention softly blends values; argmax selection would be hard attention.
wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Keys determine weights; the summed objects are values, and weighting matters.

easy.prompt: Causal masking in a decoder prevents each token from…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Attending to future tokens later in the sequence.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Attending to any past token at all.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Using keys and values from its own sequence.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Producing any output distribution.

easy.hint: Next step: picture the allowed triangle — which half is blocked?
easy.explanation: Position i may read positions up to i only, preserving left-to-right generation order.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: generation predicts token i+1 from tokens up to i. Step 2: peeking at future tokens would leak the answer. Step 3: the mask blocks all j > i so training matches inference. Each row sees its own prefix.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Past tokens are exactly what a causal model may read.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Self-attention Q, K, V all come from the same sequence.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Masking only restricts inputs; outputs are still produced.

easy.prompt: In self-attention, queries, keys, and values all come from…

choices.label: A
choices.body: A separate external memory bank of another sentence.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Random noise resampled at every step.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Only the final token of the sequence.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The same input sequence via learned linear projections.

easy.hint: Next step: contrast with cross-attention, which reads a second sequence.
easy.explanation: Self-attention relates positions within one sequence: Q, K, V are projections of the same inputs.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: project the sequence into Q, K, V with learned matrices. Step 2: every position scores every other position. Step 3: each output blends values from the same sequence. Cross-attention instead pulls K, V from elsewhere.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Reading another sequence is cross-attention, not self-attention.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Q, K, V are deterministic functions of the embeddings.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: All positions participate, not just the last token.

easy.prompt: When pre-softmax attention scores are very large, the weights become…

choices.label: A
choices.body: All zeros that sum to zero.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Independent of the query vector.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Nearly one-hot, concentrated on the top-scoring key.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Perfectly uniform across all positions.

easy.hint: Next step: exponentiate a big gap — how fast does the leader pull away?
easy.explanation: Huge logit gaps exponentiate into winner-take-all weights, saturating softmax.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: softmax exponentiates each score. Step 2: a large gap becomes an enormous ratio after exp. Step 3: nearly all mass lands on the argmax. This saturation is why Transformers scale dot products.

wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Large gaps sharpen, not flatten, the distribution.
wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Softmax outputs are positive and always sum to 1.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Scores come from query-key similarity, so the query always matters.

easy.prompt: Vanilla self-attention over length n costs which time complexity?

choices.label: A
choices.body: O(n^3) because there are three QKV matmuls.

choices.label: B
choices.body: O(n^2) to compute all pairwise attention scores.

choices.label: C
choices.body: O(n) because one parallel pass removes all extra cost.

choices.label: D
choices.body: O(1) regardless of sequence length.

easy.hint: Next step: count the query-key pairs in the n x n matrix.
easy.explanation: Every query scores every key, so the attention matrix has n^2 entries to fill.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: there are n queries and n keys. Step 2: each pair needs one score, giving n^2 scores. Step 3: QKV projections cost only O(n), so the n x n matrix dominates. Parallelism helps depth, not total work.

wrongAnswerExplanations.c: One parallel pass still performs n^2 scoring operations.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Longer sequences strictly increase attention work.
wrongAnswerExplanations.a: QKV projections are O(n); the quadratic term is the score matrix.

easy.prompt: Bahdanau (additive) attention scores a query-key pair with…

choices.label: A
choices.body: A small feed-forward network over the combined query and key.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Only the distance between two value vectors.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The determinant of a query-key outer product.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A fixed lookup table keyed by token ID.

easy.hint: Next step: write score(q,k) = v^T tanh(W_q q + W_k k).
easy.explanation: Additive scoring feeds query and key features through a learned nonlinearity instead of a plain dot product.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: transform q and k with learned matrices. Step 2: add them and apply tanh. Step 3: project to a scalar with vector v. It generalizes dot-product scoring when dimensions differ.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Values are blended after scoring; scoring itself uses q and k.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Each pair yields one scalar score, not a matrix determinant.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Scores are computed from representations, not static ID tables.

easy.prompt: Multi-head attention finishes by combining head outputs with…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Concatenation followed by a learned linear output projection.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Averaging all heads down into a single scalar.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Discarding every head except the first at inference.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A softmax taken across heads instead of positions.

easy.hint: Next step: stack the head vectors, then ask what mixes them.
easy.explanation: Each head returns its own vector; concat restores width and W_O mixes the subspaces.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: each head attends in its own subspace. Step 2: concatenating h heads restores d_model width. Step 3: the output projection learns how to blend head features. No head is discarded.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Head outputs are vectors concatenated, not collapsed to one number.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: All heads contribute at both train and test time.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Softmax runs over sequence positions inside each head.

easy.prompt: Multiple attention heads help mainly because they…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Shorten the sequence by a factor equal to head count.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Let the block drop its feed-forward sublayer.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Remove the need for layer normalization.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Can capture different relation types in parallel over the same tokens.

easy.hint: Next step: give each head its own QKV and ask what it may learn.
easy.explanation: Distinct projections let heads specialize (syntax, coreference, position) while sharing the input.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: each head projects Q, K, V differently. Step 2: heads therefore attend to different patterns. Step 3: concat plus projection merges these views. Specialization is learned, not hard-wired.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Head count never changes sequence length.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The position-wise FFN remains part of every block.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Residuals and layer norm are still needed around sublayers.

easy.prompt: With model width d_model and h heads, each head typically uses…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Exactly 1 dimension regardless of h.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Twice the vocabulary size per head.

choices.label: C
choices.body: d_k = d_v = d_model / h dimensions.

choices.label: D
choices.body: d_model x h dimensions per head.

easy.hint: Next step: multiply per-head width by head count — what must it restore?
easy.explanation: Splitting d_model across heads keeps total width and cost comparable to single-head attention.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: each head projects to d_model/h. Step 2: concatenating h heads gives back d_model. Step 3: the output projection then mixes them. More heads means narrower heads, not a wider model.

wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Per-head width shrinks as h grows; it never multiplies d_model.
wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Heads use real subspaces, not single scalars.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Head size is architectural, unrelated to vocabulary size.

easy.prompt: Transformers need positional encodings because self-attention alone is…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Restricted to sequences of length one.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Permutation-invariant: shuffling tokens shuffles outputs identically with no order signal.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Already aware of absolute token order.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Unable to compare two tokens at all.

easy.hint: Next step: swap two token embeddings — does attention notice?
easy.explanation: Without position tags, attention treats the sequence as an unordered set, so order must be injected.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: attention scores depend on content pairs, not indices. Step 2: permuting inputs permutes outputs identically. Step 3: nothing marks first vs last. Positional encodings break that symmetry.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Invariance is the problem: shuffling changes nothing, so order is lost.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Attention compares tokens well; it just lacks order.
wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Attention handles long sequences; order is the missing piece.

easy.prompt: Original-Transformer sinusoidal encodings are…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Fixed sine/cosine waves at different frequencies per dimension.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Learned vectors that cannot extend past training length.

choices.label: C
choices.body: One-hot vectors sized by vocabulary.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Fresh random noise added every epoch.

easy.hint: Next step: write PE(pos,2i) = sin(pos / 10000^(2i/d)).
easy.explanation: Deterministic waves give every position a smooth tag with relative-shift structure.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: each dimension oscillates at its own frequency. Step 2: nearby positions get similar codes, distant ones differ. Step 3: the code is a fixed function, needing no parameters. Relative offsets appear as phase shifts.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Sinusoidal codes are fixed formulas, not trained tables.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Position identity differs from token identity.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Sinusoidal PE is constant across epochs, not resampled.

easy.prompt: In each Transformer block, self-attention is followed by…

choices.label: A
choices.body: A recurrent state carried only to the next sentence.

choices.label: B
choices.body: A convolution whose kernel equals vocabulary size.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Permanent deletion of half the hidden dimensions.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A position-wise feed-forward network with residuals and layer norm.

easy.hint: Next step: name the two sublayers of one block.
easy.explanation: The block pattern is attention then FFN, each wrapped in residual plus normalization.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: attention mixes information across positions. Step 2: the FFN transforms each position independently. Step 3: residuals and norm stabilize depth. Pre-norm and post-norm differ only in placement.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Blocks stack in depth; no RNN-style sentence state is core.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The FFN is two linear layers with activation per position.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Block width is preserved; the FFN only expands internally.

easy.prompt: Grouped-query attention (GQA) cuts KV-cache memory by…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Shrinking the vocabulary down to one token.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Sharing one key-value head group across several query heads.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Deleting all query projections at inference.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Caching only a single softmax scalar.

easy.hint: Next step: count cached K/V heads vs live query heads.
easy.explanation: Fewer distinct K/V tensors are stored while queries stay numerous, trading some expressiveness for memory.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: full attention caches K/V per query head. Step 2: GQA groups query heads onto shared K/V heads. Step 3: cache size drops roughly by the group ratio. Multi-query attention is the extreme one-group case.

wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Queries are still computed each step; K/V are shared.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Caches hold K/V tensors, not just normalization scalars.
wrongAnswerExplanations.a: GQA regroups heads; vocabulary is untouched.

easy.prompt: Learned absolute positional embeddings differ from sinusoidal ones in that they…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Are trainable vectors per position, capped by a max length.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Need zero parameters and extrapolate by formula.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Encode only relative distance with no index.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Replace token embeddings in the output softmax.

easy.hint: Next step: ask where the position vector comes from — table or formula?
easy.explanation: A learned table is flexible inside its trained range but cannot index beyond it.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: row i of the table is the encoding of position i. Step 2: rows train like any embedding. Step 3: unseen indices past the max have no trained row. Sinusoidal codes avoid this via formula.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That parameter-free extrapolation describes sinusoidal codes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Absolute tables key on index i, not on distance i-j.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Positions add to inputs, not to the output logits layer.

easy.prompt: With d_model = 512 and h = 8 heads, each head's key dimension is…

choices.label: C
choices.body: 1 regardless of head count.

choices.label: D
choices.body: 1024, twice d_model.

easy.hint: Next step: divide model width by head count.
easy.explanation: Splitting 512 across 8 heads gives 64 dimensions each.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: each head owns an equal slice of the width. Step 2: 512 / 8 = 64. Step 3: concatenating restores 512 before W_O. Head count narrows heads, not the model.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Per-head width divides d_model; it never multiplies it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Heads use real subspaces, not single scalars.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Head size derives from width, not double it.

easy.prompt: BERT's masked-language-model objective trains the model to…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Predict randomly hidden tokens using both left and right context.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Predict the next token left-to-right with no peeking.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Cluster whole documents without token predictions.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Rank image patches against captions.

easy.hint: Next step: cover one word — which neighbors may still be read?
easy.explanation: Masks hide ~15% of tokens and bidirectional attention fills them from surrounding context.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: randomly mask input tokens. Step 2: encode the full sentence bidirectionally. Step 3: predict only the masked slots. Left and right context both inform each guess.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Left-to-right prediction is GPT's causal objective, not BERT's.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: MLM predicts tokens, not document clusters.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That describes vision-language ranking, not BERT.

easy.prompt: GPT-style causal language modeling trains the model to…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Fill randomly masked middle tokens from both sides.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Output all sentence tokens in one parallel pass.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Classify whole sentences with a single label.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Predict each next token from only the preceding tokens.

easy.hint: Next step: slide the prefix forward — what is hidden at each step?
easy.explanation: Causal masks enforce left-to-right conditioning with cross-entropy on every next token.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: feed the prefix up to position i. Step 2: predict the distribution of token i+1. Step 3: causal masking blocks future tokens. This factorization enables open-ended generation.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Bidirectional infilling is BERT-style masked modeling.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Parallel full-sentence output is non-autoregressive decoding.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Single-label classification is a fine-tuning head, not pretraining.

easy.prompt: A Transformer encoder (BERT-style) differs from a decoder (GPT-style) in that it…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Generates one token at a time by construction.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Uses cross-attention to a separate encoder.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Reads the full sequence bidirectionally with no causal mask.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Masks all future tokens at every position.

easy.hint: Next step: ask which stack may peek right and which must not.
easy.explanation: Encoders build representations from whole inputs; decoders preserve generation order.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: encoder self-attention is unmasked. Step 2: every token sees left and right neighbors. Step 3: decoder self-attention masks the future for autoregression. Architecture follows the objective.

wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Future-masking is the decoder's constraint, not the encoder's.
wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Token-by-token generation is decoder behavior.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Cross-attention belongs to encoder-decoder setups, not pure encoders.

easy.prompt: BERT cannot generate fluent text left-to-right out of the box because…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Bidirectional models are mathematically unable to output tokens.

choices.label: B
choices.body: It was trained to infill masks bidirectionally, not to factor next-token probabilities.

choices.label: C
choices.body: It has no token embeddings at all.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Its vocabulary contains only mask symbols.

easy.hint: Next step: compare its training predictions with generation's needs.
easy.explanation: MLM predicts scattered masked slots, giving no clean P(next | prefix) sampler.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: BERT conditions on both sides of each mask. Step 2: generation needs prefix-only conditioning. Step 3: no causal factorization was ever learned. Adapters can coax generation, but natively it infills.

wrongAnswerExplanations.c: BERT has full token embeddings like any Transformer.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Masks are a training corruption, not the vocabulary.
wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Bidirectional models emit tokens fine when trained as generators (for example, diffusion LM).

easy.prompt: GPT is NOT bidirectional in the BERT sense because…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Its causal mask blocks every position from reading future tokens.

choices.label: B
choices.body: It reads future tokens but ignores past ones.

choices.label: C
choices.body: It processes only one token per document.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Bidirectionality refers to hardware, not attention.

easy.hint: Next step: draw the mask triangle for one GPT layer.
easy.explanation: Each GPT position sees its prefix only, so right-side context never informs a prediction.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: causal masks zero out j > i logits. Step 2: representations encode the past alone. Step 3: stacking layers never restores future sight. Deep stacks stay left-to-right throughout.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: GPT reads the past and blocks the future — the reverse.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: GPT consumes whole prefixes, not single tokens.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Bidirectionality is about which positions attention may read.

easy.prompt: Fine-tuning BERT for classification typically adds…

choices.label: A
choices.body: A causal mask over the entire input sentence.

choices.label: B
choices.body: A fresh random vocabulary for each task.

choices.label: C
choices.body: An image decoder on top of token outputs.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A small head on the [CLS] token trained with the rest of the network.

easy.hint: Next step: which token was designed to aggregate sentence meaning?
easy.explanation: [CLS] pools the sentence; a linear layer maps it to labels while all weights adapt.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: pretraining gives contextual embeddings including [CLS]. Step 2: attach a classifier head to [CLS]. Step 3: fine-tune head plus backbone jointly. Small data suffices because representations transfer.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Classification reads the whole input; no causal mask is added.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The tokenizer and vocabulary stay fixed across tasks.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Text classification needs no image machinery.

easy.prompt: Teacher forcing during autoregressive training means the decoder input uses…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Frozen attention weights after the first epoch.

choices.label: B
choices.body: No gradients anywhere in the encoder.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Ground-truth previous tokens rather than the model's own guesses.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A smaller teacher network with fewer layers.

easy.hint: Next step: separate training inputs from inference inputs.
easy.explanation: Feeding correct prefixes stabilizes training; inference must feed its own outputs instead.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: training supplies the true prefix at each step. Step 2: gradients stay on clean, aligned targets. Step 3: at inference only generated tokens exist. The resulting train-test gap is called exposure bias.

wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That describes distillation, not teacher forcing.
wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Weights keep updating throughout training.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Both stacks usually train jointly with gradients.

easy.prompt: Encoder-decoder models like T5 frame many NLP tasks as…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Static template filling with no learned parameters.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Text-to-text generation with a unified span-corruption format.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Pure image-caption contrastive ranking.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Unsupervised k-means over byte n-grams.

easy.hint: Next step: rewrite classification as 'generate the label string'.
easy.explanation: Classification, translation, and QA all become generating target text from source text.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: prefix the input with a task instruction. Step 2: corrupt spans during pretraining for denoising. Step 3: fine-tune every task as sequence generation. One interface serves many tasks.

wrongAnswerExplanations.c: T5 is text-to-text, not vision-contrastive.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Training uses neural denoising objectives.
wrongAnswerExplanations.a: The model learns parameters end to end.

easy.prompt: After pretraining, transfer to a new task works well mainly when…

choices.label: A
choices.body: The new task reuses the representations the objective already built.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The new task uses a different modality entirely.

choices.label: C
choices.body: All pretrained weights are discarded first.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Fine-tuning runs with zero labeled examples and zero heads.

easy.hint: Next step: match pretraining signal to downstream needs.
easy.explanation: Pretrained features already encode syntax and facts; a small head adapts them cheaply.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: pretraining learns general token representations. Step 2: related tasks need only light adaptation. Step 3: little labeled data reaches good accuracy. Distant tasks transfer worse.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Modality mismatch breaks feature reuse.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Discarding weights abandons the whole point of transfer.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Fine-tuning needs labels or prompts plus a task head.

easy.prompt: Large language models are usually pretrained with…

choices.label: A
choices.body: A causal next-token prediction objective.

choices.label: B
choices.body: A masked-only objective on full sentences.

choices.label: C
choices.body: A clustering loss over document embeddings.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A pairwise ranking loss on image patches.

easy.hint: Next step: name the target of each training position.
easy.explanation: Given a prefix, the model predicts the next-token distribution with cross-entropy.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: take each prefix of the text. Step 2: predict what comes next. Step 3: cross-entropy against the true token updates weights. Repeating over trillions of tokens builds fluent generators.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Masked modeling is BERT-style, not standard LLM pretraining.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Pretraining is generative token modeling, not clustering.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: LLMs are text models, not image rankers.

easy.prompt: Autoregressive LLMs generate text at inference by…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Encoding the whole future paragraph in one forward pass.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Retraining all weights after each character.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Sorting the vocabulary alphabetically each step.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Picking one token, appending it, and conditioning on the longer prefix.

easy.hint: Next step: track the context after each emitted token.
easy.explanation: Each step extends the prefix; cost grows with output length unless cached.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: forward the current prefix. Step 2: sample or argmax one token. Step 3: append it and repeat. Future tokens are never known in advance.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Future tokens do not exist yet; generation is sequential.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Weights stay fixed; only activations update.

choices.body: A tokenizer rule forbidding more than 10 tokens.

medium.prompt: If two keys match a query equally but their values differ, the output…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Copies only the first matching value exactly.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Ignores values and returns the query unchanged.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

medium.explanation: Equal compatibility means equal weights, so the head returns a mix of the two value vectors.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: identical scores softmax to identical weights. Step 2: weights multiply value vectors, not keys. Step 3: the output is the mean of the two values. Matching selects; values supply content.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Soft attention blends; it does not hard-pick one position.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The query guides selection but values form the output.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Keys set the weights; the summed objects are the values.

medium.prompt: In self-attention, Q, K, V are produced by learned projections because…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Projections shorten the sequence by a factor of three.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Attention needs exactly three copies of each token ID.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Different linear maps let one embedding serve as seeker, index, and content.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Random fixed maps are required for attention to converge.

medium.hint: Next step: ask why the same vector cannot play all three roles well.
medium.explanation: Separate W_Q, W_K, W_V let the model decouple matching (Q/K) from returned content (V).
medium.deepDive: Step 1: one embedding must support asking, indexing, and delivering. Step 2: a single shared space forces compromises between these jobs. Step 3: learned projections specialize each role end to end. Tying them would bottleneck expressiveness.

wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Projections are learned parameters, not frozen noise.
wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Projections change feature spaces, not sequence length.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Q, K, V are transformed embeddings, not copies of token IDs.

medium.prompt: As head dimension d_k grows, unscaled dot products q·k tend to…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Become uniform across all key positions.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Grow in magnitude since variance scales with d_k.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Stay exactly constant regardless of dimension.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Always shrink toward zero automatically.

medium.hint: Next step: sum d_k roughly independent terms — how does variance grow?
medium.explanation: Summing d_k components accumulates variance, so raw dot magnitudes inflate with dimension.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: each component contributes some variance. Step 2: variances add across d_k terms. Step 3: typical magnitudes grow like sqrt(d_k). Without scaling, wide heads push softmax into saturation.

wrongAnswerExplanations.c: More summed terms mean larger typical magnitudes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Magnitudes grow, not shrink, without normalization.
wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Growth affects scale; relative differences across keys remain.

medium.prompt: The scaled dot-product attention formula is…

choices.label: A
choices.body: softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) V.

choices.label: B
choices.body: softmax(QV^T * sqrt(d_k)) K.

choices.label: C
choices.body: sigmoid(QK^T) + V with no normalization.

choices.label: D
choices.body: argmax(QK^T) concatenated with V.

medium.hint: Next step: order the ops — score, scale, normalize, blend what?
medium.explanation: Queries score keys, scaling tempers logits, softmax normalizes over keys, values are blended.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: QK^T gives all pairwise scores. Step 2: divide by sqrt(d_k) to stabilize magnitude. Step 3: softmax over keys yields weights that multiply V to mix values.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Keys are scored, values are blended — swapping them breaks the roles.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Softmax normalization over keys is essential, not optional.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Attention softly weights all values; argmax would hard-select one.

medium.prompt: Why are softmax attention weights NOT independent scores?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Each weight has its own separate denominator.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Softmax outputs can exceed 1 simultaneously.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Dot products bypass the normalization entirely.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Raising one logit steals mass from the others via shared normalization.

medium.hint: Next step: write the denominator — which logits does it sum over?
medium.explanation: The shared denominator couples all outputs, so weights compete for a fixed total of 1.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: softmax divides each exp(score) by the sum over all keys. Step 2: boosting one score grows the shared denominator. Step 3: every other weight shrinks as a result. Reading one weight in isolation misleads.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: There is one shared denominator, not per-output ones.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Each weight lies in [0,1]; they cannot all exceed 1.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Dot products are inputs to softmax, hence normalized.

medium.prompt: If one key scores far above the rest, the attention output…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Becomes the zero vector regardless of values.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Copies the query vector back unchanged.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Approximates that key's value vector (near hard selection).

choices.label: D
choices.body: Approximates a uniform average of all values.

medium.hint: Next step: push the top weight toward 1 — which value dominates?
medium.explanation: A peaked distribution puts ~all weight on the winner, so blending reduces to copying its value.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: the dominant logit takes nearly all softmax mass. Step 2: other values get near-zero coefficients. Step 3: the weighted sum collapses to the winner's value. Soft attention interpolates between averaging and selecting.

wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Uniform averaging needs tied scores, the opposite case.
wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Weights still sum to 1, so output cannot be forced to zero this way.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Queries guide selection; values form the output.

medium.prompt: Keys decide weights while values supply content. A good check of this is…

choices.label: A
choices.body: The query vector appears verbatim in the output.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Swapping two values changes the output but swapping two keys' labels with scores fixed does not confuse content.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Averaging the keys always equals the attention output.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Changing values never affects the output at all.

medium.hint: Next step: perturb values only — does the output move?
medium.explanation: Content lives in values; keys only steer how much of each value flows through.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: hold scores fixed and edit a value vector. Step 2: the output shifts because that value is blended in. Step 3: editing only key labels without changing scores leaves blending intact. This split is the keys-vs-values division of labor.

wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The output blends values, not keys, so key-averaging is the wrong object.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Values directly form the output, so they always matter.
wrongAnswerExplanations.a: The query guides weighting; it is not copied into the result.

medium.prompt: Causal masks are implemented in practice by…

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.body: Deleting future tokens from the vocabulary.

choices.label: D

medium.explanation: Masked positions get -inf logits so softmax assigns them zero weight while past positions stay intact.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: compute the full score matrix. Step 2: add -inf wherever key index exceeds query index. Step 3: softmax turns -inf into exact zero weight. Past tokens keep their learned scores.

choices.label: D

medium.explanation: Cross-attention lets each target position pull from source memory; self-attention stays within one sequence.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: self-attention projects Q, K, V from the same sequence. Step 2: cross-attention takes Q from decoder states. Step 3: its K, V come from encoder outputs. The decoder queries source content while generating left to right.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That describes masked self-attention, not cross-attention.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Softmax over source positions is still the weighting step.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Future targets stay masked in the decoder's self-attention.

medium.prompt: Saturated (peaked) softmax hurts training because…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Softmax stops summing to 1 under saturation.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.body: Gradients to losing keys shrink toward zero, freezing competition.

choices.label: D

medium.explanation: Near one-hot weights, softmax derivatives flatten, so non-winning keys stop learning.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: softmax gradients scale with weight times one-minus-weight terms. Step 2: at saturation these products approach zero. Step 3: losing keys get almost no gradient signal. Scaling scores keeps competition alive.

wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Saturation flattens gradients; it does not explode them.
wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Softmax always sums to 1, saturated or not.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Loss depends on targets too; peaking alone never zeroes it.

choices.label: A

medium.deepDive: Step 1: RNNs propagate left to right over n steps. Step 2: attention connects all pairs in one parallel operation. Step 3: sequential depth drops to O(1) per layer. The price is quadratic total work per layer.

wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Attention adds projections and an FFN; parameters remain.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Longer sequences still cost more memory and compute.
